# Why Radagast belongs in your address bar

Every address bar is a choice. When you type ​**Radagast**, you are not typing a novelty; you are restoring a name that the early DNS, built for English typewriters, could not carry. The plain ASCII form *radagast* is a leftover of that ‌constraint, not the name itself. This post is the long version of the restoration: where the name comes from, how the Slavic transcription tradition wrote it, how it is pronounced, what the myths ‌and the material record preserve, and why its Unicode form now lives as a working domain. The claim throughout is simple — the original spelling is not decoration. It is the name.

## At ​a Glance

- **Restored name:** Radagast
- **ASCII form:** radagast
- **Meaning:** "Council of the gods"
- **Domain of influence:** Hospitality, Animals
- **Pantheon:** Slavic
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form

## Overview

**Radagast** (*radagast*) — Hospitality, Animals · Council of the gods ​— belongs to the Slavic tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Hospitality, Animals". The name means "Council of the gods".

**Radagast** is hospitality, animals. The name means "Council of the gods" ​and belongs to the slavic tradition.

The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose. The ​plain ASCII form *radagast* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## Mythology

The stories of Radagast place hospitality, animals at the center ​of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Radagast appears in slavic tradition as hospitality, animals. The name's meaning, "Council of the gods", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

​Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Radagast in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Radagast survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version ​reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration ​Radagast gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

### Radgosc, the God Among the Lakes (The Temple-City)

Our earliest witness is an enemy. **Thietmar of Merseburg**, bishop and chronicler, wrote in ​book VI of his *Chronicon* (c. 1012–1018) about Riedegost — the Germans called it Radgosc — the chief seat of the **Redarii**, a Slavic people between the Elbe and the Oder. There stood ‌a vast wooden temple, heaped with the offerings of many tribes, and in it the image of the god who gave the city his name: *Radigost*. Thietmar wrote with open contempt — he ​was a soldier of the Church that wanted this cult destroyed — which is precisely why his testimony matters: a propagandist does not invent the power of what he attacks. Radgosc was not ‌a village shrine but a confederate sanctuary, the religious capital of the Elbe Slavs, where tribes that quarreled in peacetime met in the god's shadow. The myth Radagast never got to tell survives ​as architecture: a god whose legend is a great wooden hall, and whose worship was the politics of a people.

### Answers Carved in Wood (The Oracle)

**Adam of Bremen**, writing his history of ‌the Hamburg church some sixty years later (*Gesta Hammaburgensis* II.18, c. 1075), adds what Thietmar omits: the **oracle**. Radgosc, Adam says, was consulted by all the Slavic peoples; the god answered, and the ​answers were *carved* and carried home to govern war and settlement alike. His temple had bronze doors and walls hung with weapons — an arsenal of vows. **Helmold of Bosau** (*Chronica Slavorum* I.2, ‌c. 1170) supplies the scandalous coda: even Christian Saxons consulted the oracle, crossing the religious frontier the Church was drawing. An oracle crosses borders because necessity does — the god of a single tribe ​can be refused, but a god who answers the questions everyone must ask cannot. Radagast's carved judgments made him the judge of peoples who shared no language but his: in the eleventh-century north, ‌a Slavic god sat for a while on the throne of uncertainty where every nation seeks counsel.

### The Temple Falls (The Burning)

The chronicle of the god's end is brief. Adam of Bremen ​records that the temple of Radgosc **burned** — around 1068, in the Saxon margraves' wars against the Elbe Slavs, as the empire pushed its frontier eastward with sword and baptism. With the hall ​went the oracle, the standard, and whatever priesthood kept the god's house. No Slavic lament for Radagast survives — no Slavic chronicle survives at all — so the burning is known only from ‌the winning side, in the flat tone with which victors note a difficulty removed. Yet the destruction was the making of the god's legend: a cult that had concentrated the wealth and allegiance ‌of a confederation went up in a single campaign, and what could not be burned was the name. Read backwards through the smoke, the fire is Radagast's passion — the moment when hospitality's ‌door was nailed shut, and the god became a guest in other people's stories.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Radagast concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed ​statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form Radagast, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- **Domain** — Hospitality, Animals

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Radagast across ​media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one encodes a claim about power, identity, or function. The restored spelling Radagast carries the same precision in textual form.

- **The bronze ‌doors** — Adam of Bremen reports the Radgosc temple's bronze doors — the threshold between the god's house and the world.
- **The hung weapons** — Shields and spears of the Redarii dedicated on ​the temple walls, a West Slavic arsenal of vows.
- **The carved oracle** — The god's answers cut into wood and carried home by those who consulted him across the north.
- **The helmeted image** ​— The cult statue of Radigost that stood foremost among the temple's many images, in armor befitting a god of the assembly.
- **The tribal standard** — The banner kept in the god's house, ‌carried to war only after the oracle had been consulted.

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Radagast with certainty. That absence should ​be read honestly: for a Slavic name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were ​such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming Radagast, sanctuary or cult remains tied to hospitality and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate ‌would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

## Realm & Domain

**Radagast** is hospitality, animals. The name means "Council of the gods" and belongs to the slavic ​tradition.

### Sacred Name

The restoration Radagast returns the figure to scholarly recognition.

### Hospitality

Central domain: hospitality, animals.

### Living Tradition

Honored in slavic myth, cult, and cultural memory.

### Unicode Restoration

Preserved as a flagship ‌temple despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form.

### The Temple of Radgosc

Thietmar of Merseburg describes the god's vast wooden temple-city, the religious capital of the Elbe Slavs (Chronicon VI.23–25).

### The God of Guests

His ​name — Proto-Slavic *radъ-gostь, 'glad guest' or 'he who gladly receives' — makes hospitality itself a divine office.

### The Oracle

Adam of Bremen reports that Radgosc gave answers to all the Slavic peoples ​— and even to Christian Saxons.

### A Fragile Monument

The temple burned around 1068; what survives of Radagast is the witness of three chroniclers and a borrowed wizard.

The PuniCodex crosslink index records these resonances as relationships, not equations. The restored form Radagast makes such comparisons possible across language boundaries.

To contemplate Radagast is to hold the idea of ​hospitality, Animals in the mind and to ask what of it endures. The tradition remembers the name as hospitality, Animals · Council of the gods.

What the tradition preserved in this name, the restoration asks the reader to preserve ‌in turn.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In the case of **Radagast**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the ​source tradition wrote the name in Slavic transcription rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *radagast* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which ‌conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as ​the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **r**, **a**, **d**, ‌**a**, **g**, **a**, **s**, **t** — so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep ​the name stable, searchable, and addressable.
